articles.title: Inside the Bitcoin Mining Bug That Traps Slow Machines
articles.content: Bitcoin is, at its core, a record of who owns what. To better explain, no one is in charge of it. There is no bank behind it, nor is there a company sitting in the middle to oversee the activities. Instead, thousands of computers around the world, called nodes , each keep their own full copy of the record. Think of a notebook that everyone in a town keeps a copy of. When you pay someone in Bitcoin, you are not necessarily handing over a coin, you are pretty much announcing a new line to the network, something like "this amount now belongs to Ada", and node who hears it checks it against the rules. Was the money really yours to spend? Have you already spent it somewhere else? If the line breaks the rules, they ignore it and do not pass it on. If it passes, they pass it along and keep it ready to be written down. That is the whole point of the design. Everyone who runs a node can verify the record independently. You do not have to trust a bank to tell you what you own, because you can check the record yourself. But there is a problem with having thousands of independent computers maintaining the same record. What happens when two people try to spend the same bitcoin at roughly the same time? Some nodes may hear about the first transaction before the second, while others receive them in the opposite order. Each node can only accept one of the conflicting transactions, but how does the network eventually agree on which one counts? Without a bank to settle the disagreement, who decides which payment is valid? And why should anyone trust the answer? Bitcoin's answer is proof of work . Rather than allowing anyone to decide which transactions make it into the record, the network requires participants to demonstrate that they have performed computational work. Transactions are collected into batches called blocks , which you can think of as pages in our notebook. Roughly every ten minutes, a miner proposes the next page, and other nodes check it against the rules before accepting it. Each new page also refers to the one before it, so the pages form a chain in a fixed order. When two transactions conflict, the network eventually settles on the one included in the accepted chain. The other is rejected. Putting a page together, however, is not free. If anyone could write the next page, they could include whatever transactions they wanted and expect everyone else to copy it. The rules therefore require miners to prove that they have spent real computing effort before their proposed block can be accepted. That proof of work is what mining produces, and the people doing it are called miners. So what does that effort actually look like? A miner takes a candidate block containing pending transactions, adds an extra number to it, and runs the entire thing through a hash function. This number, called a nonce , can be changed repeatedly. Each time the block is hashed, the result is a fixed-length string that looks random. Change even one character of the input and the output changes completely. There is no reliable way to predict which number will produce the result the network needs. The network only accepts a block if its hash, interpreted as a number, falls below a target set by the protocol . The miner has to keep changing the nonce and trying again until it finds a result that meets the requirement. Mining machines do this trillions of times every second. That speed is called the hash rate . It is a bit like rolling dice until a very rare combination turns up. Finding it takes an enormous number of attempts and a lot of luck. Checking the result, on the other hand, takes just one roll. Once a miner finds a valid block, other nodes can verify it independently. The successful miner receives newly created bitcoin as well as the fees from the transactions included in the block. At the time of writing, that reward is 3.125 bitcoin per block . articles.title: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench
articles.content: Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6 , a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200 . Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. How does harness distillation move the gains into weights? Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. What do the benchmarks show? The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Test score Database Codebase Spectrum Average No memory 7.5 31.8 21.9 20.4 Compaction 39.8 36.9 34.6 37.1 Generic harness 32.3 33.5 42.5 36.1 Best human-written 47.9 43.7 42.1 44.6 Optimized harness 53.8 64.3 49.9 56.0 SFT on generic trajectories 31.6 37.5 43.6 37.6 SFT on optimized trajectories (generic prompts) 37.7 45.1 46.5 43.1 Source: Figures 4 and 5, Self-Improving Memory blog . Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across…

articles.title: Second iOS 27.3 and macOS Golden Gate 27.3 Public Betas Now Available
articles.content: Apple today seeded the second betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS Golden Gate 27.3, tvOS 27.3, and watchOS 27.3. Apple also has revised betas of of iOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3 available for developers. iOS 27.3 is a major update that adds a Vertical Tabs layout option and Adaptive Dark Mode for Safari. Siri AI can do more in and across Apple's apps, and developers are now able to create actions for ‌Siri‌ to carry out. In the second developer beta , Apple introduced a facial unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front camera, along with an option to lock the ‌iPhone Duo‌ when it's closed. The redesigned Health app is now available with custom Insights and Longevity information, and the ‌iPhone Duo‌ supports Reachability. There's a new Selfie Sing feature in Apple Music , plus changes to StandBy on non-Duo iPhones. Apple has started testing Apple Intelligence and ‌Siri‌ AI usage limits, with extra access available through iCloud + plans. A full list of what's new in the beta can be found in our guide . On the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Audio Intelligence features Live Rewind and ‌Siri‌ Recap are available for testing. Live Rewind creates a transcript of the last 15 seconds of speech, and ‌Siri‌ Recap offers a high-level summary of conversations throughout the day. ‌macOS Golden Gate‌ 27.3 has the same Safari features, and it brings Live Activities to Macs without a Dynamic Island . To get the new betas, you can sign up on Apple's beta testing website . After you're signed up, the betas can be installed through the Software Update section in the Settings app on each device. We're expecting all of Apple's updates to launch in December. articles.title: Google just gave Gemini the run of your Mac — three days after Apple tightened the rules
articles.content: Google is adding computer use to its Gemini app for macOS. The assistant can now work across desktop applications and websites in a separate background window without taking over the user’s screen. Gemini handles tasks in the background while users continue working. The feature includes a live preview in the chat so users can monitor the agent’s activity, pause execution, and approve actions when necessary. The company’s announcement Thursday comes just three days after Apple introduced tighter permission controls for macOS automation. The company’s announcement Thursday comes just three days after Apple introduced tighter permission controls for macOS automation. Google hasn’t explained how Gemini will operate under the new restrictions. Apple tightens agent permissions The macOS 27.3 beta 2 changes split Device Control and Data Access permissions into two categories; System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. Apps requesting broad system access will face more explicit permission prompts, and users can approve individual requests instead of granting ongoing access. Developers building desktop agents will also need to account for least-privilege access , since users can restrict or revoke permissions while an agent is running. Gemini’s new Mac powers Google says Gemini can extract shipping details from local PDFs, gather dashboard metrics for presentations, edit batches of photos, and work with 3D design software. The company hasn’t detailed how the background environment is isolated from macOS, how it maintains state across applications, or which actions require user approval. Google’s existing computer-use API Google introduced computer use with Gemini 2.5 in October 2025 and later integrated it directly into Gemini 3.5 Flash. According to the developer documentation , the model works from screenshots and returns actions for client-side execution. Developers manage the execution environment, while the API provides configurable safety policies, and optional screenshot scanning for prompt injection. The new Mac feature is part of the consumer Gemini app, not a separate developer API. The new Mac feature is part of the consumer Gemini app, not a separate developer API. It’s unclear whether the app uses the same execution architecture or whether Google plans to open its background environment to third-party developers. Where Google stays silent The company has documented prompt-injection safeguards for its developer-facing computer-use tools but hasn’t said which protections are built into the Mac app. Agents with access to local files and privileged applications also risk untrusted input reaching the agent harness , and influencing the actions it executes. Reliability questions remain unanswered since the company has not shared any performance figures for the Mac app or explained what happens when an action fails, or an application behaves unexpectedly. Reliability questions remain unanswered since the company has not shared any performance figures for the Mac app or explained what happens when an action fails, or an application behaves unexpectedly. Rollout, requirements and tiers Gemini computer use is rolling out in English in the United States for personal Google accounts belonging to users 18 and older. The feature requires an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. articles.title: New Windows 11 lock screen zero-day unlocks BitLocker-protected PCs with just a few keystrokes
articles.content: Considering the current status of the cybersecurity landscape, some may well say that "0-day" has lost its meaning, The latest high-stakes vulnerability pertains to a bug in Windows 11 (and possibly 10), wherein an attacker can partially bypass the lock screen and run software as the logged-in user, and seemingly access their data. If true, the vulnerability means even BitLocker won't help keep users' files protected. Unsurprisingly, the bug was discovered by Abdelhamid Naceri, the prolific Windows hacker known to the world as Nightmare Eclipse, and is responsible for about a dozen zero-day findings in Microsoft's operating system. The exploit requires physical access to the machine, but that's precisely the scenario that lock screens and/or BitLocker are supposed to protect against. To trigger the vulnerability, all you need is a keyboard. In the Windows 11 lock screen, click "Forgot my PIN," then hit Win+U to bring up the voice narrator. The window will be hidden behind the lock screen, which, for practical purposes, is just a veneer, but you can interact with it using the keyboard if you hold down the Caps Lock key and use the arrows and Enter. After some brief navigation through Narrator, you'll actually be in Settings, and then have multiple avenues for further shenanigans. One obvious one is going into Bluetooth and Devices and setting Autoplay to show a USB stick's files and folders, then plugging in your own with your software of choice to run. Additionally, on a personal machine, the user is bound to have administrator permissions, so you can just create your own account. This bug is quite fresh, so there isn't widespread reporting or testing. The author claims "the vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in." We did encounter a sysadmin on Reddit, danrhodes1987, who claims they've tested it on machines they manage, and sure enough, it works, though only on their InTune-enrolled devices. He says that "you can launch anything you want in the context of the user logged onto the device." Additionally, they found it possible to invisibly navigate whichever programs the user had open before they locked their screen, which all but guarantees that the victim's entire data and programs will be fully accessible. As a Windows sysadmin friend of mine remarked, Windows' lock screen implementation always felt like a kludge, and he posits this won't be the last hack found for it.

articles.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
articles.content: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio . Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token. Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle. Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use. SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result. In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring. Solution overview SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action. Observe – Monitoring of latency and capacity usage is on by default for eligible endpoints. It doesn’t read your requests or responses, and it carries no additional GPU cost. Notify – When there is something worth acting on, you receive a plain language notification in AWS Health, plus email, explaining what was observed, why it matters, and a recommended next step. Recommend (opt in) – One selection opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker Studio, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic, so you can benchmark alternatives on separate compute. Decide – Compare response time, throughput, and cost side by side. Production is not changed until you apply a result. The feature produces a few types of findings. The…

articles.title: What Happens When AI Makes So Many Decisions That We Forget How?
articles.content: A personal investigation into how AI is changing our reflexes, our tolerance for effort, and eventually the decisions we still call our own. The most important thing AI may be changing is not what we know. It is what we do in the first few seconds after we realize we do not know something. That sounds trivial, but I think it may be the beginning of a much larger behavioral shift. For most of my life, uncertainty triggered a small sequence of actions: remember who might know, search for the right words, open several sources, compare them, decide what seems plausible, and only then act. Increasingly, one new reflex compresses that sequence into a single gesture: ask the AI. A strange symptom. A recipe for whatever is left in the kitchen. The name of an actor I can almost remember. A confusing bill. A message I do not know how to phrase. A question about whether a laptop is actually worth the extra $300. These are not spectacular uses of artificial intelligence. That is precisely why I find them more interesting than the demos. Technologies change a society most deeply when they stop feeling like technologies and become habits. Search engines did that once. They gave us the phrase “just Google it,” and eventually we stopped hearing how strange that sentence was. AI is producing a new version: “just ask it.” The next phrase may be even more consequential: “just let it handle it.” This essay is about what happens in the space between those three sentences. Before “Just Google It,” Questions Had a Price For most of history, information had friction. You asked someone who might know. You checked a manual or an encyclopedia. You went to a library. You waited until you could speak to a doctor, mechanic, teacher, salesperson, or relative who had dealt with the same problem. Even when the answer existed, getting to it cost time, attention, and often a little embarrassment: you had to admit to another human being that you did not know. The internet collapsed much of that cost. Search engines taught an entire generation a new cognitive skill: translate the messy question in your head into keywords, scan results, ignore obvious junk, open several tabs, compare sources, and assemble an answer from fragments. We outsourced access to memory, but we still did much of the interpretation ourselves. A famous 2011 Science study by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu, and Daniel Wegner found that when people expected information to remain available, they were less likely to remember the information itself and more likely to remember where it could be found. Later work on cognitive offloading described the broader pattern: humans routinely move mental work into notebooks, calendars, calculators, GPS, phones, and other parts of the environment. There is nothing inherently unhealthy about this. Civilization is, in part, a history of building tools so the brain does not have to carry everything alone. But Google still left one important burden with us. It gave us routes to information. It usually did not decide which route deserved our trust. That distinction is where generative AI begins to feel different. AI Is Changing the First Reflex, Not Just the Answer With conversational AI, I no longer have to think like a search engine. I can ask the question the way it exists in my head, incomplete and slightly confused. The system can ask a follow-up, infer what I am trying to accomplish, summarize competing possibilities, and turn scattered information into something that feels like an answer. That changes more than convenience. It changes the first move. Instead of entering an information landscape and navigating it, I hand the landscape to an intermediary. The difference is subtle because the screen still looks like a place where I type words. Psychologically, however, the task has shifted from retrieval toward delegation of interpretation. For readers who want the technical layer behind this shift, I have a separate explainer on how modern AI systems work .…

articles.title: Building MCP Servers for My Own Products: Introducing the Workflow
articles.content: I used to manage my products through dashboards. Check analytics here, schedule posts there, pull metrics from another tab. Constant context-switching. Now, I do all of it by talking to Claude. Not through some hacked-together integration: through MCP servers I built for my own products. Model Context Protocol is the standard Anthropic published for giving AI assistants structured access to external tools. I built servers for both Spellcast and Lunary. Here's how, and why it changed everything. What MCP actually is (in one paragraph). MCP is a protocol that lets you define a set of "tools", which are functions with typed inputs and outputs that Claude can call during a conversation. Instead of copy-pasting data into a chat window, Claude calls your API directly and works with the live result. The architecture: your MCP server exposes tools over stdio (or HTTP). Claude Code discovers them and can call them when relevant. You write the server once; it works in any MCP-compatible client. The Spellcast MCP Spellcast is my social scheduling platform. The MCP server exposes the full API as typed tools: server.addTool({ name: 'list_posts', description: 'List scheduled, published, draft, or failed posts with optional filters', parameters: z.object({ account_set_id: z.string().optional(), status: z.enum(['draft', 'scheduled', 'published', 'failed']).optional(), limit: z.number().default(50), }), execute: async ({ account_set_id, status, limit }) => { const posts = await db.query.posts.findMany({ where: buildWhereClause({ account_set_id, status }), limit, }); return posts; }, }); What I can do from a Claude conversation: list_posts : see everything in the queue create_post : schedule new content update_post : edit scheduled posts publish_article : push articles to Dev.to and Hashnode get_analytics : pull engagement data list_brand_voices / update_brand_voice : manage AI personas generate_content : create post variations using my brand voice list_account_sets : manage posting personas The practical workflow: I describe what I want, and Claude calls the tools. "Optimize the hooks on my scheduled tweets" becomes Claude reading every post, identifying weak openers, and rewriting them in batches. The Lunary MCP Lunary is my astrology platform. The MCP exposes product analytics and content tools: server.addTool({ name: 'get_dashboard', description: 'Get key product metrics: MAU, MRR, retention, feature usage', parameters: z.object({}), execute: async () => { const metrics = await getProductMetrics(); return metrics; }, }); What I can do: get_dashboard : MAU, MRR, retention at a glance get_dau_wau_mau : engagement breakdown get_feature_usage : which parts of the app people actually use get_cohort_retention : how well I'm holding users over time search_grimoire : search the 2,000+ article content library get_ai_insights : patterns Claude surfaces from the data predict_churn : identify at-risk users What the workflow actually looks like A typical morning: Me: "Check Lunary metrics and tell me what's changed since last week." Claude calls get_dashboard , get_dau_wau_mau , get_cohort_retention . Returns a summary. Surfaces what moved. Me: "Schedule a thread about the SEO growth for the sammii account." Claude calls list_account_sets to find the right persona, get_brand_voice to load my voice profile, generate_content to write five thread variations, presents them, waits for my pick, then calls create_post to schedule it. Me: "Those tweets from February with weak hooks, fix them." Claude calls list_posts for the date range, reads each one, identifies weak openers, writes improvements, calls update_post in batches. No dashboards. No tab-switching. Just conversation with full product access. articles.title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
articles.content: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions? Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create q uestions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently . Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths. We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-le d, structured interviewing. Three core design principles 1. Build interviews around job-related evidence Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover. The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience. 2. Separate interviewing from scoring Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passa ges. The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. 3. Build fairness protections into the design Connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information. What the research shows To understand how well the se design principles work in practice, we combined independent I-O psychology evaluations with internal research. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency. Connect Talent keeps interview questions focused on job-relevant skills The quality of a structured interview starts with the skills it measures. Candidates need questions that reflect the requirements of the role, and hiring teams need confidence that the…

articles.title: MAHA PAC spent more on steak, luxury club than candidates, report shows
articles.content: In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement's midterm wipeout , a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA's own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group's priority was ever winning elections in the first place. The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates. The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA's clout in the midterms . In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously. articles.title: Chase, Visa, Mastercard confirm third-party cyberattacks that may have exposed customers' info
articles.content: JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants. “Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday . “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.” Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach. “We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.” JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register ’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media. “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.” According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday. None of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions. Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®
articles.author: Jessica Lyons

articles.title: AI data center power demand will double by 2030 thanks to $4 trillion in spending, adding an entire Great Britain to energy strain
articles.content: The AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 report , a total of 120GW of capacity is currently available across all types of data centers across the globe, with another 120GW expected to be completed by the end of the decade, 75% of which would be dedicated to artificial intelligence. Aside from that, it’s also tracking 93 large “AI factories” that are either under construction or being expanded via satellite imagery. It estimates that the capacity for these sites grew from under 2GW to 17GW in just two years, and that they’re expected to hit a total of 50GW upon completion, the equivalent of adding a second Great Britain to power demand. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible This massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices. However, the IEA says that its analysis “does not yet show a clear relationship between growth in data center capacity and increases in electricity prices.” It noted that if a data center uses existing capacity and pays for its share of the cost, then it could potentially lead to lower utility bills for all customers. However, if the grid operator is required to upgrade its system to accommodate the large consumer, then it could also lead to increased monthly bills if the costs are spread across all users. Emissions are another issue that the IEA has raised. Renewable energy dominates data centers’ power purchase agreements at nearly 50%, but actual power generation puts coal- and natural-gas power sources closer to 60%. This is likely due to the need for reliability, with the latter kicking in when the former cannot deliver the power that the data center needs. Aside from that, a few projects are deploying their own power, like Elon Musk’s Colossus 2 in Southaven, Mississippi , with about 180GW planned or under construction in the U.S. So, even though renewable energy is growing to accommodate demand, it’s also expected that coal- and natural-gas emissions from data centers will rise by 70% by 2030. Investments in AI data centers are expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, putting the infrastructure spending for the industry larger than railways, electrification, and the internet, combined. Despite that, the IEA says the grid remains a significant bottleneck — renewable power plants take between one and five years to complete, which is around the same time that some massive data center projects take if they do not face an extended moratorium, while transmission works can take three to five times longer. This is probably one of the reasons why some AI hyperscalers are choosing to put jet engines on their sites instead, although these are also facing shortages, especially in turbine blades .

articles.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
articles.content: PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code. "An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it
articles.content: A worker moves a cart of packages at an Amazon delivery station. New York City’s proposed Delivery Protection Act would require companies running last-mile facilities to directly employ their delivery drivers. (Amazon Photo) Amazon and New York City are fighting again. The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill. The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518 , would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered. Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February. On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported . Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure. In a blog post , Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.” Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers. In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said. “We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning. The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives. Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way. It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections. We are crafting legislation that regulates…

articles.title: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next
articles.content: Microsoft employees eligible for the Voluntary Exit Offer have until early December to decide. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide , laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically . Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances. Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept . Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year. The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer. All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires. The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you. I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now? Question 1: How easily can I get another job? Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy. There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI. One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems. But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role. It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company. “It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.” Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day. The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now. AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era. Product management, program…
articles.author: Nikesh Parekh

articles.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
articles.content: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor. Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday . He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.” Evasive and irregular turns “FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.” Read full article Comments
articles.author: Dan Goodin
articles.fingerprint: company defense feds hired man russia say silicon spied tech valley

articles.title: An engineer didn’t message his AI for 22 of 44 days. It built an Android app anyway.
articles.content: Cognition has spent nearly three years developing Devin as an autonomous engineer that takes a ticket and ships a pull request. With Tuesday’s launch of Devin Bots , the company is moving into management, introducing persistent agents that oversee multiple Devin coding sessions, and take responsibility for engineering outcomes over days or weeks. Coordination becomes the product CEO Scott Wu argues that eliminating even a small amount of remaining human work could produce outsized productivity gains. In a post on X , he asks how much more developers could accomplish if coding agents went from handling 98% of their work to 99%, and says Cognition had seen enormous differences among beta testers and internal teams. The percentages are hypothetical, but Wu is making the case that coordination, not just coding, is the next opportunity for automation. The percentages are hypothetical, but Wu is making the case that coordination, not just coding, is the next opportunity for automation. From tickets to targets Cognition founding team member Silas Alberti described the change in a post on X as a move toward assigning agents ongoing goals instead of individual tasks. He says the team has already used Devin Bots to compress weeks of research into days. The company shares the example of keeping an Android app in sync with its iOS version. As new features are added to iOS, a Devin Bot can assign the corresponding Android work without an engineer having to create a ticket for every update. The idea builds on a trend toward coding agents that function as team members . Devin Bots takes that a step further by putting an agent in charge of coordinating the work. An Android app, barely supervised When the company set out to build an Android version of Devin, it had no dedicated Android engineers. Instead, the company assigned the project to a Devin Bot on September 28 and let it coordinate the coding work. Over the next 44 days, Cognition says the Bot merged 1,134 pull requests, wrote 344,651 lines of Kotlin and closed 1,217 tickets. It also ran 2,841 screenshot tests. The engineer overseeing the project sent 183 messages during that period, including none on 22 of those days. In its write-up , Cognition explains that the Bot opened tickets and assigned them to individual Devin sessions, then merged changes once they passed continuous integration and Devin Review. The team could follow along through daily Slack updates that included screen recordings. The Android app is now in open testing on Google Play, though it still needs work before it matches the iOS version. Cognition’s Layout Bot checks the company’s web app for visual bugs every three hours, rebuilds the latest production code, and tests the interface under different loading conditions. Engineers merged 159 of its fixes over three weeks, reducing layout lag by 70%, according to Cognition. Cognition says the studio went from producing around 50 pull requests a week to 1,900. A mobile game studio also has roughly 20 bots reporting to another agent named Super Jenny. Four times a day, Super Jenny brings decisions to a human operator. Cognition says the studio went from producing around 50 pull requests a week to 1,900. Where oversight runs thin Multiple coding agents working on the same project can introduce conflicting dependencies or bugs that affect other agents’ work. Cognition hasn’t explained how Devin Bots handle those conflicts. Tasks requiring approval go to a “Needs You” inbox for an engineer to review. Developers can protect specific CI checks and set compute spending limits before assigning a project to a Bot. Tasks requiring approval go to a “Needs You” inbox for an engineer to review. The company hasn’t disclosed how the supervising Bot decides when code is ready to merge or when repeated failures warrant human intervention. articles.title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
articles.content: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman. Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed. The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Google's Gemini Can Now Control Apps on Your Mac
articles.content: Google today expanded Gemini's capabilities, allowing it to take full advantage of your Mac. Gemini for Mac can use apps, files, and websites to complete multi-step tasks in the background while you work in the foreground. According to Google, Gemini can do repetitive work, handling clicking, typing, menus, and forms. It works in an isolated window with a live preview in the Gemini chat interface so you can keep an eye on what it's doing. You can choose the apps that Gemini can use, and it will ask for approval before taking "key actions." Google suggests Gemini's new feature is useful for batch editing photos, preparing listings for resale platforms, and turning metrics and screenshots into a presentation. The new option for Gemini to take control of a Mac is available before macOS 27.3 launches , so the timing is convenient. With the update, Apple will warn users about the dangers of giving apps unrestricted access to their data, making it clearer exactly what AI agents will be able to see and do. Apple will let users limit access to specific apps and folders and configure apps to get permission each time access is requested. There's also a transparency indicator that makes it clear when an app is controlling another app. Users who install apps asking for Mac permissions now won't have to re-grant those permissions after macOS 27.3 is released, nor will users see the new explanation screens Apple is putting in place. Gemini for Mac can be downloaded from the Google website . Computer use is available to Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers in the U.S., with the plans starting at $4.99 per month. The app requires an Apple silicon Mac. Tags: Gemini , Google This article, " Google's Gemini Can Now Control Apps on Your Mac " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Google brings computer use to Mac, letting Gemini handle chores without hijacking your screen
articles.content: TL;DR Google is rolling out computer use to the Gemini app for Mac, allowing it to operate desktop apps and websites on your behalf. Gemini works in an isolated background window, leaving your screen and cursor free while you monitor its progress in real time. The feature requires an Apple Silicon Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription, and is initially available in the US. When Google brought Gemini Spark to the Mac earlier this year, it gave its AI assistant access to local files, allowing it to handle chores like organizing folders and turning documents into spreadsheets. But working with files on your computer and actually operating the apps installed on it are two different things. Google’s latest Gemini update bridges that gap. Just two days after making Gemini Tasks available for free and adding the ability to call businesses, make purchases, and accept requests via text and email, Google is rolling out computer use to the Gemini app for Mac . The feature, which we first learned was in testing in September , lets Gemini click buttons, type, navigate menus, and fill out forms across desktop apps and websites on your behalf.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge

articles.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
articles.content: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands capabilities, on AWS Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment. A more capable managed harness Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults: A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence. Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior. Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost. Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses . Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context…

articles.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
articles.content: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. articles.title: Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz
articles.content: As AI has become a thorn in the side of the security industry, Palo Alto Networks (PAN) has reached an agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI model training platform. "We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the company's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday. "The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks." So in the spirit of "hair of the dog that bit me," PAN is ingesting Applied Compute to make open-weight AI more secure for corporate customers. The answer to insecurity brought on by AI is buying security with AI. In its announcement of the tie-up, PAN declares "the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs." That view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. His resignation as CEO of Nvidia has led to worries that the open-weight ecosystem has lost some lobbying power at a time when the US is wary about the uptake of models made in China. Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models. "Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional." The company expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029. Arora, on the company's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data. "We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he said. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year." Beyond the sticker price, PAN is ready to up its infrastructure ante. Arora said the biz expects to build infrastructure supporting more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity, a project that will take "a modest CapEx commitment of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030." ®

articles.title: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains
articles.content: Blue Origin announced Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company's Project Suncatcher program. Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research "moonshots." The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy. "Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit," said Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release. "This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what's possible for the future of compute." Read full article Comments

articles.title: Gemini can now control Mac apps, but you still shouldn't let it
articles.content: Google's Gemini can now control Mac apps and edit files on your behalf, but the convenience comes with security risks serious enough to make handing over that control a bad idea. Gemini and Apple Intelligence Google announced computer use for its Gemini Mac app on November 19, expanding the assistant's ability to complete multi-step tasks across local files, desktop apps, and websites. The feature builds on the company's existing Mac app by letting Gemini perform actions instead of simply helping users prepare them. Users can describe a task, and Gemini will navigate menus, click buttons, enter information, and move between apps to finish it. Google suggests using the feature to batch-edit photographs or extract information from PDFs to complete shipping forms. Gemini works in a separate virtual screen, leaving the main display and cursor available for other work. A live preview shows what the agent is doing, and users can stop the task at any time. articles.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
articles.content: The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday , the FCC argues the rule will help combat an "influx of contraband cellphones" used to carry out crimes from prison. Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934 , though they're used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. articles.title: International Men’s Day: Anthropic IPOs, Trump Meets Putin and Xi, and GTA 6 Is Released
articles.content: Image Credit, @Rational_Answer November 19, 2026. Three of the world’s most powerful men meet to discuss nuclear weapons. An artificial intelligence company raises more money in a single IPO than most countries spend on technology. And millions of men finally get to steal fictional cars in Vice City. Happy International Men’s Day. An ⁠ excellent Venn diagram circulating on X captured the extraordinary coincidence of three events occurring on November 19, 2026. The three circles: Anthropic IPO GTA 6 release Trump, Xi, and Putin meet The overlaps: Anthropic + GTA 6: “$80+ to play” Anthropic + world leaders: “AI chips discussed” GTA 6 + world leaders: “Men doing stupid shit” And in the center: November 19, 2026. Someone in our HackerNoon Slack channel pointed out the final coincidence: it’s International Men’s Day. The joke is funny enough on its own. But the more you investigate the actual news, the stranger the connections become. Elon Musk thinks AI might eventually generate games like GTA without traditional developers. Anthropic’s CEO believes advanced AI chips should be kept away from China. Trump thinks whoever wins the race to superintelligence wins everything. Meanwhile, the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers are discussing how not to destroy civilization. And Rockstar Games has just released a video game about committing crimes. Let’s examine this particularly remarkable day in the history of men. 1. Anthropic Goes Public: $83 to Play On November 18, Anthropic announced that it had ⁠ priced its initial public offering at $83 per share. The offering comprised 980 million shares, representing approximately $81.34 billion in gross proceeds before expenses and excluding any additional shares sold through the underwriters’ option. Not all of that money goes to Anthropic. Approximately 23.6 million shares were being sold by existing stockholders. Nevertheless, it was an extraordinary amount of money. When Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19, shares opened at $111.50. That’s approximately 34% above the IPO price. As ⁠ Barron’s reported when trading began , investors who received shares at the offering price immediately found themselves holding something worth considerably more. The $83 price also happens to be almost identical to the price of GTA VI. The difference? For approximately $80, Rockstar gives you a fictional world where you can do almost anything. For $83, Anthropic gives eligible IPO investors a tiny ownership stake in a company trying to build artificial intelligence that might eventually do almost anything. Dario Amodei’s Very Expensive Experiment Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spent years arguing that increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could fundamentally transform society. Now public investors get to bet on that argument. In an ⁠ interview following the IPO , Amodei reflected on how rapidly the technology’s economic implications had become real: “I don’t think we really believed it until it actually happened.” His sister, Anthropic cofounder and president Daniela Amodei, characterized the IPO as another milestone rather than the destination: “it’s like one stop on the journey, right?” The company has also warned investors that its commitments to AI safety may sometimes conflict with maximizing profits. That creates an interesting question. What happens when shareholders want Anthropic to make more money, but Anthropic’s leadership believes making more money would create unacceptable risks? Senator Elizabeth Warren has already raised concerns about exposing investors and retirement savings to the risks surrounding advanced AI. In a statement ahead of the offering, she argued: “The SEC must protect investors and Congress must act quickly to put in place safeguards on advanced AI development.” The broader contradiction is difficult to ignore. Anthropic was founded partly because its creators believed advanced AI required extraordinary caution. Now it is…

articles.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
articles.content: All four colors of the WH-1000XM5 are in stock at the discounted price. Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones , which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy . While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months. Sony WH-1000XM5 Where to Buy: $399.99 $198 at Amazon $399.99 $198 at Best Buy $399.99 $199.99 at Costco The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6 , they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point. The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday ( Amazon , Best Buy ), down from their MSRP of $450. To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price. Read our Sony WH-1000XM5 review .

articles.title: You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
articles.content: Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon. The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve's waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an "add-to-cart" status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve's website . articles.title: Xbox Black Friday deals — save on Xbox games, peripherals, and more right now
articles.content: Black Friday brings the biggest gaming discounts, and that’s no different this year if you own an Xbox. There’s a slight caveat, though: the consoles — the Xbox Series S and Xbox Series X — aren’t on sale thanks to RAMageddon . That said, you can still save on discounted games and peripherals. Right now, you can get The Game Awards nominees, like Resident Evil Requiem for $39 at Amazon . Meanwhile, Pragmata is another fantastic Capcom title discounted by $20 . Peripherals-wise, the standard Xbox controller is $20 off , while the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 5X is $99 . Finally, you can get a 12-month Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscription for $5 off . Whether you’re new to Xbox or just want to build out your gaming library, now is the best time to do so. Not only because of Black Friday deals, but also because of the awesome games on the Xbox horizon. Here are the latest Xbox Black Friday deals. I’ll update this post regularly, so be sure to check back for the latest savings! Firstly, it comes in an attractive Robot White hue, and it also lacks a disc drive, so it is designed solely for digital play. It's the perfect console for Xbox Game Pass players. Packed with chaos, fun, and a bit of a learning curve, CrossWorlds shines with smooth drifting and air tricks that deliver significant boosts. View Deal The latest game in the Mafia series takes you back to 1900s Sicily, the birthplace of organized crime. You play Enzo, a fresh recruit in the Torrisi crime family, and must work your way up the ranks to become a "made man." Offering a narrative-driven campaign packed with third-person firefights and high-speed chases (in cars and on horseback), Mafia: The Old Country is a highly engaging action-adventure game. But the game struggles to balance its two playable protagonists, and player choices are still inconsequential. Though it doesn’t take risks, its thrilling gameplay and stunning graphics keep you engaged from beginning to end. It proves that there's still innovation in the AAA space and is yet another winner from Capcom. This is a game that humans and androids alike can enjoy.
