articles.title: Where should AI workloads run? Probably next to the data.
articles.content: AWS raised prices on EC2 Capacity Blocks , its reserved GPU capacity, by about 15% in January and about 20% in July . Picture a platform team watching a training job’s bill climb after copying a few hundred terabytes of sensor data across regions just to reach the GPUs, then realizing the data never had to move. For AI workloads, the real question is whether the workload goes to the data or the data goes to the workload. Data gravity usually answers it. Data gravity hits AI workloads harder than it ever hit analytics Data gravity is the tendency of compute, applications, and services to be pulled toward large concentrations of data, because moving the data costs more than moving the logic that processes it. The larger a dataset grows, the more expensive every copy becomes, and the more everything that needs that data ends up living next to it. Scheduled BI often tolerates periodic queries against sampled or aggregated data. Large training runs can require repeated reads of a much larger dataset, while agents retrieve fresh context throughout a workflow. When those reads cross regions or environments, transfer costs and latency add up. Each agent output also becomes new data that feeds the next round of retrieval, which compounds the pull over time. A January 2026 analysis in BigDATAwire argued that AI workloads removed the cushion that let enterprises leave data gravity unmanaged for a decade. The year’s pricing moves make the same point from the cost side. Combined, the two increases add up to roughly 38% on the H200 instances that took both. Moving data to the compute stops working at AI scale Centralizing compute can require copying data into its environment before a job starts, and that transfer may carry charges. For illustration, assume a transfer rate of $0.02 per GB and a 300 TB dataset (300,000 GB). The transfer alone would cost $6,000 per copy. That’s a hypothetical, not an AWS quote. Real charges depend on source, destination, route, service, and terms, so cross-region and cloud-to-premises movement needs explicit costing. Remote reads also add network latency, which matters when a workload has a tight response-time target. “Transfer bills, duplicate pipelines and the engineering hours spent maintaining them belong in the placement calculation alongside compute charges.” Two more costs rarely show up next to the GPU rate: Interoperability overhead: cross-environment pipelines need their own translation layers when engines, query languages, connectors, and software development kits (SDKs) differ. Lock-in: transfer charges and the engineering work of moving data and pipelines can make leaving an environment expensive. Transfer bills, duplicate pipelines and the engineering hours spent maintaining them belong in the placement calculation alongside compute charges. Moving compute to the data instead A scheduling and placement layer can send a job to an environment that already holds its data, avoiding repeated full-dataset transfers. The job still needs compatible accelerators, enough memory, a supported runtime, and adequate storage throughput. Model weights, container images and checkpoints may also need to move. Making that decision well means evaluating four inputs together, every time a job is scheduled: Input What to evaluate Cost The total cost of this job in each candidate environment, including compute, transfer, storage, and queueing, at current prices. Data gravity How much data the job needs, where it sits, and what it would cost to move. Residency Which jurisdictions the data and the job are allowed to touch. Policy Which access rules, classifications and quality gates apply wherever the job lands. A placement layer first excludes environments that violate residency or access rules, then compares feasible options by capacity, performance, and total cost. It dispatches the job with its runtime policies and revisits placement when those conditions change. Where a specific workload belongs depends on the…

articles.title: Russian national accused of stalking San Francisco techie in plot against US defense-tech giant
articles.content: A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes. Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent. After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company. Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war. While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir , which did not respond to our request for confirmation. D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July. The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees. In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device. The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims. D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so. One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong. D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots. The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler. Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date. Inside recruitment The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations. According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US. Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram. A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp. The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically…

articles.title: How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments
articles.content: Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself. AWS has built all of those capabilities directly into Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS), so you don’t have to. “Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself.” You can access all these tools through a single API endpoint. AWS built them to work out of the box when you use Amazon ECS as your container orchestration platform with the Amazon ECS deployment controller. As a result, you don’t have to build your own abstractions or learn a new framework to get the deployment behavior you want. Instead, you pick and choose the features you want through a service deployment configuration and update it as your needs change. How the building blocks map to ECS If you’ve run progressive delivery on Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts or Flagger , you know the shape of the stack: a controller you install and keep current, analysis wired to your metrics backend, and a traffic provider for weighted canaries. Argo Rollouts approximates canary weights with replica counts and uses an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger uses a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries, and plain Kubernetes Services for blue/green. Both are mature open-source projects and a great fit when you want to own and tune every layer. ECS takes a different approach and builds the same capabilities into the service. Here’s a comparison of the different deployment controllers: What you need With Argo Rollouts or Flagger (Kubernetes) Built into ECS Deployment strategies Rolling updates come with Kubernetes Deployments; blue/green and canary come from a controller you install and keep current Rolling, blue/green, linear, and canary, set in the service’s deployment configuration Traffic shifting Argo Rollouts: replica-count weighting by default, or an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger: a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries ECS shifts traffic through your ALB, NLB, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice, or calls your own logic through lifecycle hooks Health and metric analysis Analysis templates or built-in checks against your metrics provider (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch, and others) Deployment circuit breaker plus CloudWatch alarm monitoring Automatic rollback The controller aborts and shifts traffic back to the stable version when analysis fails ECS rolls back on circuit breaker or alarm, and you can pull the cord yourself with the StopServiceDeployment API Custom checks and approval gates Webhooks, custom analysis steps, or manual promotion Lifecycle hooks with Lambda or pause targets, resumed with the ContinueServiceDeployment API When are rolling deployments not enough? Rolling deployments are where ECS started, and they’re still the right default for most customers. In a rolling deployment, ECS replaces tasks running the old version with tasks running the new one, a batch at a time. New tasks start receiving production traffic as soon as they pass health checks, and ECS stops old tasks as the new ones take over. Two settings, minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent, control how many tasks can be replaced at once and how much extra capacity the deployment can use. Rolling deployments work with both the deployment circuit breaker and CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, which we’ll cover below. So, where’s the gap? By the time your alarm fires, a large share…

articles.title: The best things in open source are built together
articles.content: In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion , more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities. Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine. Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica , an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework . I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed. This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked: “What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?” John replied: “I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.” Replica, a new open-source design harness In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica , which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit. GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground John Maeda, CVP GitHub & CoreAI Design With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate. With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit. A11y Framework, a new open-source accessibility framework Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all. As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer. Ed…

articles.title: Europe's biggest gas supplier battling cyberattack – with no timeline for recovery
articles.content: Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the company insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production. Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen. In an update on Wednesday, the company said it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details. "As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The company added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers. In a further update on Thursday, Equinor said the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the company. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police. What kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or said when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored. The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network. Equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the company hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down. Equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the company. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries. The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the company also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide. Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale . The agency said the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies. Europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises. Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®

articles.title: What does the Anthropic IPO mean for your 401(k)?
articles.content: You may have no interest in investing in AI companies, and you may even suspect that the AI boom is a bubble about to pop . But you could already have a stake in one of the industry’s biggest players anyway: Anthropic, which went public today, may be in your retirement account or about to show up there. Some mutual funds, including American Funds Growth Fund of America (AGTHX) and Fidelity Select Technology (FSPTX), hold substantial equity stakes in Anthropic. And some index funds will also soon acquire shares, after recently changing their rules to make it easier for massive companies to join shortly after going public. Previously, companies often had to wait months or a year to be included in major indexes, in part because of concerns about stock volatility. Earlier this year, ahead of the SpaceX IPO , Nasdaq shortened its waiting period from three months to 15 trading days for qualified mega-IPOs. Nasdaq argued that companies as large as SpaceX and Anthropic shouldn’t have to wait so long. FTSE Russell has similarly shortened its waiting period to just five trading days, though inclusion depends on how many shares are available for public trading. Morningstar already had a short five-day waiting period, but relaxed its rules about available shares. The S&P 500, meanwhile, still requires companies to wait 12 months and turn a profit before joining—two hurdles Anthropic has yet to clear. When Anthropic is included in a retirement portfolio, it won’t have a large weight initially, Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer at Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity at Vanguard, tells Fast Company . That’s because a relatively small portion of the company’s shares will be available to public investors to begin with. Vanguard has estimated that Anthropic will represent 0.05%–0.15% of its total market index fund. If you have $500,000 in that fund, that might mean $250 to $750 worth of indirect exposure to Anthropic. How to find Anthropic in your 401(k) To know if your 401(k) or an index fund you own will include Anthropic, you’ll have to dig into the details. “Most people don’t look at their index funds, or anything that their 401(k) is invested in,” says John Polonis, a former Wall Street lawyer who now writes about finance. Even if you’ve chosen not to invest in the Nasdaq-100, for example, the stock could still be hiding somewhere else. Other funds, including those that invest in the largest publicly traded companies, could also hold Anthropic shares. “There may be ways that you are getting exposure,” Polonis says, “and if you don’t want any exposure at all, you really have to do a lot of diligence to kind of screen that.” To check your own portfolio, log into your 401(k) account. If you have actively managed mutual funds, look up each fund’s portfolio holdings and search for Anthropic. If you have index funds, check to see which indexes they track. The indexes that will soon acquire Anthropic stock include Russell 1000, Russell 3000, Nasdaq-100, Morningstar U.S., FTSE Global All Cap, and MSCI USA. Because companies like Alphabet and Amazon also own large chunks of Anthropic stock, index funds also have exposure through those companies. The risk for passive investors is low at this point because exposure is limited. But exposure is likely to grow over time. And some critics argue that because Anthropic is still at an early stage, and not yet profitable, it shouldn’t be part of retirement accounts. Jonathan Westin, executive director of Climate Organizing Hub and part of a group called Stop Funding Billionaires that protested in front of Anthropic’s offices in advance of the IPO, argues that the company’s early investors stand to reap enormous profits while ordinary investors shoulder the risk if the AI boom collapses. “They’re all just trying to get paid out and get paid out now before the collapse,” he says. “And then the real people that are…

articles.title: Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear
articles.content: Zeno Power’s prototype Stirling generator undergoes testing in Washington state’s waters. (Zeno Power Photo) Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use. The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer. “It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire. Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder. For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel . Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades , primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers . But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said. Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release . “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.” Zeno Power’s electrically heated Stirling generator is set for deployment from a boat in open water near the Washington state coast. (Zeno Power Photo) Zeno Power’s prototype is lowered into the water for testing. (Zeno Power Photo) Zeno test engineer Tony Messplay monitors the demonstration. (Zeno Power Photo) Zeno Power’s crew stands alongside the electrically heated Stirling generator after it was brought back to the surface. (Zeno Power Photo) Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.” Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.” “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.” Related Inside the ‘kitchen’ where Zeno Power tests radioisotope recipes Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027. articles.title: Intel continues layoffs with cuts to its IT department, hundreds of employees reportedly affected
articles.content: Intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the company's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider . The latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech . Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries , so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the company reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities. The latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the company submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider . The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported. Intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the company's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively. Intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger announced plans to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the company’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.
articles.author: Anton Shilov

articles.content: The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. scroll-state() originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.

articles.title: Microsoft positions Copilot as a hub for team collaboration
articles.content: Microsoft has unveiled Copilot Workspaces, a new collaborative environment for employees and AI agents to work together on shared projects. It was one of a range of Copilot updates at Microsoft’s Ignite conference this week, including deeper Office integration and new AI agent capabilities, as it seeks to position the AI assistant as a hub for team productivity. Workspaces replaces Copilot Notebooks, announced last year , which let users gather files and other reference materials, then ask Copilot to answer questions, draft documents, and generate audio overviews based on this content. Workspaces retains these capabilities in what Microsoft describes as a “team-first” shared space, where colleagues can collaborate on documents, with live cursors showing what they are working on. Users can also interact with Copilot, with support for Autopilot agents that work continuously in the background coming soon, too. “Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single player,” said Jared Spataro, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer, Copilot, in a blog post . “Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.” For some teams, working cooperatively on a project is a key requirement, said Jack Gold, principal analyst at J. Gold Associates. That will ultimately include agents, too, once they are considered robust and able to operate “without causing any issues that are security- or interference- related,” he said. “But for most organizations, this will be a slow uptake until it’s proven to help productivity,” said Gold. “There is significant risk that something could go wrong relying too heavily on AI capabilities.” Most organizations still use AI for individual productivity, said Max Goss, senior director analyst at Gartner, but there are signs of a shift toward “a collaborative environment where people and agents work together.” “Copilot Workspaces fits that direction well and follows what we’ve seen other AI vendors do in this space,” he said. Microsoft’s strategic goal is to position Copilot as the “front door for work,” said Goss, “bringing together people, applications, organizational context, and agents.” While such an approach could be powerful from a productivity perspective, he warned that organizations should also consider the risk of vendor lock-in. Working with agents in a multiplayer environment also introduces new data governance challenges, particularly around access controls. “If an employee shares something with an autopilot agent, how do you ensure that this agent doesn’t share with another user who shouldn’t have access?” Goss said. Workspaces is available in early access for Copilot customers on Microsoft’s Frontier program, and will roll out to Microsoft’s OneNote app “over time.” Other Copilot announcements at Ignite include Today, which provides a personalized brief each morning with an agenda of important tasks. Today, available in private preview via the Frontier program, will also prepare work for users to review and approve, such as email drafts and schedule changes. Microsoft pushes back as Anthropic and OpenAI move into office productivity market Microsoft also announced the general availability of Office in Copilot, bringing the full editable applications into the AI assistant. Office in Copilot is included in paid Copilot subscriptions, with no additional costs for document generation. The announcements follow similar moves from Anthropic and OpenAI to embed productivity tools into their AI assistant applications in recent months, with the launch of Claude Docs, Slides and Sheets , and ChatGPT’s Space and Pages . Microsoft acknowledged the competition it faces from the AI model providers at Ignite, though it claimed that the combination of Office and Copilot has an edge over its rivals’ tools. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets,” said Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president,…

articles.title: Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts
articles.content: A marketing site used to have two kinds of visitors: people and search crawlers. Now an agent can build a page, a second agent can scrape it, a third can summarize it for a potential customer, and a fourth can optimize it overnight after studying yesterday’s traffic. “The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security.” You control some of these agents but not all the data they ingest and train on. The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security. A marketing site is usually public with no login required to view or break. Adversaries go after whether the site still says what you wrote, serves what you built, and reports what real visitors did. This article calls those content integrity, delivery integrity, and signal integrity, and looks at where each kind of agent touches them. Five agents, three kinds of integrity Five agent roles show up on a marketing site today, agents that: build, read or scrape, analyze its visitor data, optimize the site from that data, adversarial agents that attack Each role touches at least one of three things worth protecting the integrity of: Content – what the site says and links to. Delivery – how that content reaches a browser, including DNS, redirects, third-party scripts, hosting, and the publish pipeline. Signal – the visitor and behavior data the site produces, plus every decision made from it. Figure 1. Where each agent role touches a marketing site, shaded cells are the primary exposure. Because the content is public, the checks that matter are integrity checks. An agent with write access can be talked into making unapproved changes, so you need governance over what it may touch and logs that show what it did. Agents that build sites Builders are usually the first agents a team adopts, so they set the pattern for every agent that follows. A builder agent writes pages, config, scripts, and redirects. The risk sits in what it reads before it writes. A doc, a ticket, a scraped competitor page, or a CMS field can carry instructions, and an agent can follow them. Recent incidents show the shape of this. In July 2025, someone slipped a destructive prompt into a pull request for the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code , and it shipped in a production version. AWS removed it and said no customer resources were affected, and reports indicate a formatting error kept the prompt from running. The same month, a Replit coding agent reportedly deleted a production database during a code freeze, despite instructions not to change anything. Replit’s response was to separate development and production databases automatically. The causes differ from provenance checks to agents stepping outside their boundaries. Figure 2. A builder agent’s path from input to publish, with the control at each stage. Read left to right. The incidents above failed at different stages of Figure 2. Amazon Q failed at the input and review stages, where untrusted text in a pull request reached a trusted release. Replit failed at the harness, where an instruction to freeze changes was the only barrier between the agent and a production database. A marketing site has the same exposure, and three layers around the agent carry those controls. The agentic SDLC is the process – where agents act across plan, draft, review, and publish, and which stages need a human decision. The agent harness is the control layer – the code around the model that decides which tools the agent can call, with which credentials, and what gets logged or approved. The sandbox is the containment layer – an isolated runtime with no standing credentials, restricted network egress, and no path to production data. For a marketing site, that translates into a few working rules. Give builder agents draft access and keep publishing behind a person. Review a…

articles.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
articles.content: Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature. The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them. The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Supermicro sued by shareholders over claims Nvidia executive’s wife knew about illicit China sales
articles.content: More information about the alleged knowledge of chip diversion by a Supermicro executive is being revealed as shareholders’ civil lawsuit against the company progresses. According to The Telegraph , the investors alleged that there was “no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge about the company’s illicit sales.” Chen, the former Chief Growth Officer at Supermicro and described by a colleague as the company’s sales leader, resigned from her position in April of this year — about a month after the three Supermicro employees, including its co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, were arrested for a $2.5-billion AI GPU smuggling scheme . Cenly Chen is married to former Nvidia Executive Vice President of Worldwide Field Operations Jay Puri, who is also described as the company’s sales chief. The Information also called him Jensen Huang’s right-hand man and said he was the person that Nvidia’s customers turned to if they wanted to buy chips or had other pressing concerns. The shareholders’ accusations and her relationship with Puri have put the former Supermicro executive in the spotlight, especially after Huang’s sudden departure from the AI chipmaker amid a flurry of affairs and smuggling accusations. Sources say that Puri controlled the AI chip allocations to server manufacturers, including Supermicro, while the lawsuit claims that Chen decided how many Nvidia racks each Supermicro customer could get. A former Supermicro employee was also quoted in the complaint saying that it was “widely known within the Company that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China.” This apparently refers to the serial numbers that were moved from real to dummy servers using a hairdryer. Supermicro has said multiple times that it has cooperated with the U.S. government regarding the smuggling investigation and that it has not been included in the lawsuit against the three defendants. Furthermore, the company has denied her involvement regarding Nvidia GPU allocations. “Chen did not manage Supermicro’s relationship with Nvidia and did not decide how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers,” a Supermicro spokesperson told The Information . They also said that she left voluntarily and that her LinkedIn profile now reads her current position as CEO of ChronoScale, an Nvidia cloud partner based in Silicon Valley. As for Puri, he stepped away from his position at Nvidia in late August, about two months before the Jensen Huang scandal blew up, although he remains as an advisor to the AI chipmaker.

articles.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
articles.content: Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026. Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States. These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year. Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project , Cloudflare for Campaigns , and Project Galileo . Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups. Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026. In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings. Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period. State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information. On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second. Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone. Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website…

articles.title: Study reveals data centers’ long-distance damage to air quality
articles.content: The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers. The team estimates that additional air pollution from the electricity demands of data centers in 2023 resulted in about 650 premature deaths across the United States. Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas. The researchers built a modeling framework that captures how the electricity demanded by data centers propagates through the nation’s interconnected power grid. The model also considers how atmospheric conditions impact the formation of air pollution in different regions. The framework identifies power plants across the country whose emissions increase in response to data center electricity demand. In parts of the Midwest, these emissions combine with atmospheric conditions that favor the formation of fine particulate matter, a pollutant that can cause heart attacks, stroke, and lung disease. The researchers say these results underscore the importance of considering unintended regional health impacts of data centers, and how the location and operations of these facilities affect public health on a broader scale. “When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy; and senior author of the study. Selin is joined on the paper by Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student; as well as others at MIT, the University of California at Irvine, and Yale University. The research appears today in Environmental Research Letters . Capturing regional impacts The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that electricity demands of data centers represented about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and resulted in about 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. That proportion has likely increased as new data centers continue to be built at a rapid pace. Many prior studies estimate impacts using average electricity-grid emissions. Like those studies, the researchers assume data centers draw power to run computing tasks 24/7. Their approach also identifies which generators respond to that additional demand hour by hour, allowing them to trace where the resulting emissions and health impacts occur, Chen explains. “Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” he says. To drill down on regional health impacts, the MIT researchers developed a modeling approach that enables them to identify which generators are contributing to data center electricity demand within each modeled region. This allows them to incorporate a spatial component into the analysis. They built an electricity system model that simulates how much electricity each generator produces and pumps into the grid every hour. This model also considers how that electricity is transmitted between regions. It gives the researchers data on emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) for each generator across the United States. articles.title: At Apple, the robots are coming
articles.content: An Industrial Automation 2026 report claims US manufacturing has spent $51 billion on robotics and automation this year. It also says spending will exceed $84 billion by 2030. It claims industrial use of robotics is moving to full-scale deployment. I’m in no doubt that Apple is part of this. “Global industrial robot stock hit roughly 5.0 million units in 2025, up 9% year-over-year, and annual installations topped 600,000 units, up 11%, per the International Federation of Robotics. China installed 354,000 of them, 59% of the global total, up from 54% in 2024,” the report states. The Association for Advancing Automation (A3) shares its own recent data that shows US companies purchased almost 11,000 robots last year, up 24.8% from the prior 12 months. “What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” A3 executive vice president Alex Shikany said. What about Apple, then? Even since Apple introduced us to Daisy , its first product disassembly robot, we have known Apple dabbles in robotics . Most recently we learned that new Apple CEO John Ternus is bullish about robotics , and we now expect the first consumer robotics products to emerge from the company in 2027 or 2028 . Apple is not named specifically in the Industrial Automation report, but several of its active partners are mentioned. Schneider Electric and Cognex are both in the Apple supply chain. The first company now manufactures Apple Home Collection products to be sold at Apple retail stores from next month. The second is thought to make specialized machine vision systems used in Apple’s iPhone display production. (Apple accounted for 20% of Cognex’s revenue in 2017 and 17% in 2018, per its SEC disclosures .) While it may not be relevant, and Cognex has not made any suggestion this is the case, it may be worth reprising that Cognex’s CFO Dennis Fehr said growth in the company’s consumer electronics business was boosted by device assembly moving outside China. He also told investors “a large consumer electronics customer” placed purchase orders through European entities for use in China and Asia. He didn’t name that customer, but it’s hard not to speculate that Apple’s continued investment in manufacturing in India may have driven at least some of that growth. After all, we know new factories require new equipment, and page 11 of Apple’s most recent supplier report confirms the use of autonomous mobile robots to help transport products and components across its factories. (Apple has been tracking robotics use across its supply chains since 2019 .) Apple has also rolled out training in robotics and other advanced manufacturing processes at its Apple Manufacturing academies, including its most recently opened one in Türkiye . Courses there cover machine learning technology, predictive maintenance, advanced automation, and robotics . (Italics mine). No manufacturing process left behind One automated manufacturing process doesn’t a summer make, but as the drive to robotics in manufacturing accelerates, Apple will not be left behind . A3 also tells us the semiconductor and electronics industry saw the highest growth in robot orders at 97.6% versus last year. (Automotive components followed at 90.4% and plastics and rubber at 67.7%. Life sciences and metals also saw strong gains at 38.7% and 37%, respectively.) Buoyed by advancements in Siri AI and the inevitable introduction of a Siri Agent AI across the Apple ecosystem, the backroom work of manufacturing will not remain a sacrosanct space for human endeavor. The robots are coming to America and will probably make Apple products there once they arrive. While Apple outsources much of its manufacturing, it also works closely with partners on the development of manufacturing processes. The ongoing litigation with OpenAI hints at the extent of that, because Apple claims OpenAI approached an Apple partner to try to learn about top-secret,…

articles.title: Developer vibe codes Windows 11 alternative operating system for amd64, arm64, and riscv64 hardware
articles.content: There’s a new vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT . Its name provides a big clue to its nature: Liber (free), NT (New Technology architecture, as in Windows NT ). As it has been released under GNU’s GPL3.0 license, LiberNT also provides a free new way to run apps designed for Microsoft’s Windows 11 . (Image credit: LiberNT ) LiberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a big leap. Reading the intro, you might have wondered if this work had a ReactOS connection, and indeed there is. But what started as a fork of ReactOS has already got a new boot loader, graphics stack, memory manager – and yesterday a new kernel . “LiberNT is not affiliated with or endorsed by the ReactOS project or Microsoft,” insist the devs behind this OS. This still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64. Ambitiously, the goal is to develop this OS to deliver a free Windows alternative that is “stable, reliable and efficient.” On that latter point, yesterday’s blog update relays some impressive efficiency and performance stats. The LiberNT team has benchmarked their eponymous OS against Microsoft’s Windows NT, and it beats it hands-down in 112 of 132 system tests. The testing assessed performance in the following areas: file caching, memory handling, threads and locks, plus FAT32 and NTFS storage. Interestingly, both the free and commercial OS were benchmarked on a Mac with an Apple M3 Pro chip. We scanned through the results, and the worst loss for LiberNT was a 28% performance deficit vs Win11, but it claims some astounding relative performance wins showing the free OS being over 2000% faster. The devs are entirely clear about the fact that the operating system was vibe coded. “AI is part of how LiberNT is built. It helps us review and write code, and everything it writes is then reviewed by a human,” explains a section of the GitHub page for the project. “Before anything reaches the main branch, a person runs and validates the end-to-end tests. We care about this project too much to let a regression slip through.” If the above highlights about this new OS's scope, mission, compatibility, and performance have whetted your appetite, there is the full code available via the GitHub link (top), and even some ready-made builds as bootable disk images. Indeed, I’m quite eager to give this new OS a spin. Hopefully, it works as well as the ambitious developers suggest, and I won’t be disappointed by any stability issues using my daily productivity apps like Firefox, Word, and an old release of Photoshop.

articles.title: The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks. They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs. Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive . —Antonio Regalado What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion. The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition. Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. articles.title: Intel 18A yields hit 70% as company signs Microsoft as EMIB customer
articles.content: Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, said on Thursday that yields of chips made using the company's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-new manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp. In addition, Intel and Microsoft have signed an agreement under which Microsoft will secure Intel Xeon supply capacity for years to come and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for in-house silicon. "When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan said at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha ). Lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon. However, it is reasonable to expect a CEO of a semiconductor company to talk about functional die yield, the percentage of dies that pass basic electrical and functional testing. Intel began volume production of compute tiles of its Core Ultra 300-series CPUs codenamed Panther Lake using 18A in the second half of 2025, so a 70% functional yield seems decent at this stage of the product ramp, though for Intel's economics a lot depends on parametric yield and how many advanced SKUs of Core Ultra 300-series 'Panther Lake' processors Intel can supply to customers at a premium. The same applies to Intel's Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest processors with up to 288 cores that are in high-volume production now and which use 18A-based compute chiplets along with Foveros Direct 3D stacking. In addition to announcing an important 18A milestone, Intel also signed a long-term agreement with Microsoft, under which the latter will secure multi-year Intel Xeon supply capacity, including supply of next-generation Xeon processors codenamed Diamond Rapids, and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for multi-chiplet data center solutions developed in-house. (Image credit: Intel) The EMIB agreement is arguably the biggest news. Microsoft is the first company to publicly commit to Intel's advanced packaging technology for its own silicon (i.e., it does not mean that Microsoft is the first third party to use EMIB; it is the first party to confirm usage of EMIB), which represents a significant commercial development for Intel Foundry in terms of publicity. However, the announcement does not identify the processors involved, their manufacturing process, production volumes, or deployment schedule. Microsoft was the first company to commit to use Intel's 18A for its data center silicon in 2024 , though it is unclear whether the newly announced EMIB packaging agreement relates to the same solution or not. As the majority of high-end data center solutions tend to use multi-chiplet design, it is reasonable to expect Microsoft's future solutions for data centers to use EMIB for multi-die processors. "Through use of our advanced packaging capabilities with EMIB to scale future generations of Azure infrastructure, Intel and Microsoft can combine the flexibility of heterogeneous integration with the manufacturing scale required for the AI era — giving customers new levels of performance and economics when interacting with Azure," said Naga Chandrasekaran, EVP, Chief Technology and Operations Officer and General Manager of Intel Foundry. The Xeon agreement provides Intel with greater visibility into future server CPU demand. Importantly, Microsoft has committed to using Intel's next-generation Xeon 'Diamond Rapids,' although the announcement does not disclose purchase volumes or financial terms. The collaboration extends beyond processor procurement and EMIB. Specifically, Intel and Microsoft are jointly developing infrastructure capabilities that encompass processor architecture, heterogeneous integration, CXL memory expansion, QuickAssist Technology (QAT) acceleration, and Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) security.

articles.title: The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities
articles.content: By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet.…

articles.title: What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course
articles.content: AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans. So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI. To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count. Top fundraisers Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers. As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks. By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor , a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation. San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers. The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob , a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce 1 -led financing. Startups focused on jobseekers Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers. In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox , an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation. Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview , a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI , which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding. Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform , announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs. Surprisingly depressing So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers? Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done. Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions. Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation. articles.title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
articles.content: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, Is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by…
